slides.headline: Getty Images Files for Chapter 11 Bankruptcy
slides.sub: The world's largest visual content archive is going private, backed by the Getty family and Koch Equity Development, as a failed $3.7B merger with Shutterstock and a $206.1M loss in 2025 forced a restructuring plan to emerge by end of 2026.

slides.headline: The Archive That Powers Generative AI
slides.caption: This is the kind of archive Getty owns — millions of images, all watermarked, all sitting idle while AI companies learn from them for free.

slides.headline: From Profit to Bankruptcy: The Timeline

steps.detail: Getty sues Stability AI for training AI on its archive without permission, demanding damages.
Getty reports a $206.1M loss; the failed Shutterstock merger leaves no capital buffer.
AI models like Midjourney give away images that once cost $500 to license.

steps.label: Oct 2026
steps.detail: Getty files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy as it can no longer pay the demanded damages.

slides.headline: The Irony of Watermarking
slides.quote: The watermark remains on every image in the archive, including those nobody is licensing anymore.

slides.headline: The Lesson for All Content Creators
slides.sub: If the world is already learning from your archive and giving it away for free, your business model may be obsolete before you even realize it.

slides.headline: Follow for more
slides.sub: Daily tech, explained.

caption:
Getty Images filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2026, emerging as a private company backed by the Getty family and Koch Equity Development. The $533M restructuring follows a failed $3.7B merger with Shutterstock and a $206.1M 2025 loss. The company had spent years watermarking every photo online, but those images remain watermarked even as they sit unused in its archive. The irony: its entire business model—owning the visual record of human history and charging licensing fees—was outrun by AI models like Midjourney that learned from that archive and gave images away for free, making the $500 licensing fees obsolete. Getty sued Stability AI in 2024 for training its AI image generator on Getty's library without permission, demanding payment. The AI companies did not pay. Getty Images filed for bankruptcy this week, citing the inability to pay the demanded damages. The story reveals a fundamental shift in how visual content is valued: from a proprietary asset that generates revenue through licensing, to a public dataset that fuels generative AI. The question is whether the old model of owning and licensing images can ever compete with AI that learns from that same archive and gives it away for free. The answer appears to be no. Getty's bankruptcy is a warning to all content creators and companies that rely on licensing models: if the world is already learning from your archive and giving it away for free, your business model may be obsolete before you even realize it. The irony is that the watermark remains on every image in the archive, including those nobody is licensing anymore. Getty's entire business model—owning the visual record of human history and charging licensing fees—was outrun by models like Midjourney that learned from that record and started giving images away for free, making the $500 licensing fees obsolete. The question is whether the old model of owning and licensing images can ever compete with AI that learns from that archive and gives it away for free. The answer appears to be no. Getty's bankruptcy is a warning to all content creators and companies that rely on licensing models: if the world is already learning from your archive and giving it away for free, your business model may be obsolete before you even realize it.
